transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Sam Ortiz (CTO, Acme Analytics), Maya Chen (Lead ML Eng), Liam Park (Eng Manager)
Recording: yes

Summary: quick discovery focused on PLG/self-serve onboarding, time-to-first-token, free credits, and evaluation path (hosted -> dedicated). Customer cares about latency/cost tradeoffs and security (SOC2, VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya our systems engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Sam: Hi Jordan, doing well. Thanks. We got about 40 minutes. Hope that's fine.
[00:10] Jordan: Perfect. Goal today is to understand your use case and get you up to speed on the quickstart - free credits, time-to-first-token, and what a pilot might look like. Priya, do you want to add?
[00:18] Priya: Yeah, I'll cover technical fit, latency expectations, and what the self-serve flow looks like plus hooks into Dedicated/Private if you need to scale.
[00:24] Maya: Quick note, we're evaluating hosted first (fastest path) but also want to scope Dedicated for predictable latency, and Private for data residency if needed.
[00:32] Liam: Also, can you confirm what's included in the free credits and how long they last?
[00:36] Jordan: Sure - our quickstart credits last 30 days and can be applied to the hosted API. They cover generation and embeddings units; we'll send the exact SKU link after the call. The goal is to get you to first token in under an hour using our SDK and example prompts.
[00:48] Sam: Under an hour sounds great, that matches our PLG playground idea - engineers should be able to iterate quickly.
[00:54] Priya: Practically, it's usually minutes: sign up, API key, pip install the SDK, run the example, you'll see tokens streaming. For more production-ish testing, you can run a small canary on Dedicated in a day or two depending on provisioning.
[01:06] Maya: When you say streaming, do you support partial responses and function call style outputs?
[01:10] Priya: Yes, streaming responses, function/tool calling, and structured output are supported. Also, we have retry/fallback policies if a model variant is unavailable.
[01:18] Liam: Cost is a concern. If we do a PLG flow and then people start hitting endpoints, what's the cost control?
[01:24] Jordan: We provide quotas, rate limits, and token-level cost breakdowns in Console. Also Optimize suggestions - batching and quantization recommendations - to reduce unit costs. For Dedicated we do reserved capacity pricing which helps predict spend.
[01:35] Sam: Our main blocker is latency for in-product features - we aim for <200ms p95 for short text generation. Can Redwood hit that on hosted?
[01:43] Priya: Short answer: depends on model and prompt shape. For smaller models and 1-2k context, hosted can deliver sub-200ms p95 in many regions; we publish performance profiles. For strict p95 targets you can move to Dedicated with pinned capacity and lower variance. We also have prefix caching and continuous batching to reduce observed latency.
[01:58] Maya: Any rough numbers you can share in email? Our SRE will want to see benchmarks.
[02:02] Jordan: We'll attach our benchmark spreadsheet and a short latency cheat-sheet. Priya, we'll include a config for an apples-to-apples benchmark.
[02:08] Priya: Yep, I'll add the benchmark config and a sample prompt set.
[02:12] Liam: Security - we handle sensitive PII. What about audit logs, KMS, and SSO?
[02:18] Jordan: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. Hosted customers get encryption at rest and in transit; for some regulated customers we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) which we can scope.
[02:30] Maya: Is Redwood SOC 2?
[02:32] Jordan: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and we can share the report under NDA. We also have ISO docs for enterprise folks.
[02:38] Sam: Great. For the pilot, we'd like to do hosted self-serve first. If we like it, we may move to Dedicated for production. Timeline target is end of Q2 to ship an initial integration.
[02:49] Jordan: That lines up. Typical pilot steps: 1) self-serve Quickstart using free credits and SDK; 2) run an apples-to-apples benchmark and share results; 3) pilot users and measure latency/cost; 4) decide Dedicated or stay hosted.
[03:03] Maya: Onboarding friction: do we need contracts for the quickstart?
[03:06] Jordan: No contracts for the quickstart. You sign up for hosted and credits apply. If you want Dedicated or Private, that's a separate procurement path.
[03:12] Sam: For the self-serve, can we set up a sandbox team and invite engineers?
[03:16] Jordan: Yes, Console supports teams and per-team keys. You can invite users and set RBAC.
[03:22] Liam: Curious about model catalog. Do you host LLaMA-style, or Open models, or proprietary?
[03:27] Priya: We host a curated catalog of open models and Redwood-verified variants. We also support folks bringing their own model artifacts in Private. For advanced customers we have recommendations on quantization and kernel selection.
[03:36] Maya: If we hit weird tokenization differences or model outputs, is there support?
[03:40] Jordan: Yes, DevRel and Solutions Eng are available; we also provide example eval harnesses and a prompt testing UI.
[03:47] Sam: Any vendor lock-in concerns? We want portability.
[03:50] Jordan: We design the platform so your prompts and model config are exportable. Private deployments further reduce lock-in because it's customer-managed.
[03:58] Maya: Ok, let's talk about time-to-first-token specifics so my engineers can estimate ramp. What will they run?
[04:03] Priya: Steps: create account, get API key, pip install redwood-inference, run the quickstart notebook. We'll provide sample env vars and a docker example. In my experience under good network conditions it's <10 minutes to first token, with realistic dev flow around 30-20 minutes to integrate into a small test harness.
[04:20] Liam: Are there SDKs for Node and Python?
[04:22] Jordan: Yes, official SDKs for Python, Node, and a simple curl endpoint.
[04:26] Maya: For the pilot we want to validate embeddings and generation. Are embeddings a separate billing unit?
[04:30] Jordan: Yes, embeddings are billed per-unit and we'll show you the SKU. The credits apply to both generation and embeddings.
[04:36] Sam: Regarding observability, can we see token-level costs per route?
[04:40] Priya: Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdown per model/route. You can also ingest traces to your APM.
[04:46] Maya: If we outgrow hosted and move to Dedicated, what's the typical lead time?
[04:50] Jordan: For standard Dedicated pools it's usually days to a couple of weeks depending on capacity and region. For Private (VPC/on-prem) the procurement/provisioning is longer - depends on networking and compliance needs.
[05:02] Liam: Any gotchas on network egress/costs?
[05:05] Priya: For Private on-prem, you're in control. For hosted, network egress is subject to cloud provider costs; we can provide guidance on placement and region.
[05:12] Sam: We'll want to run a small benchmark - 1000 requests across our typical prompt shapes, compare to OpenAI/Anthropic. Priya, can you provide the config and scripts?
[05:20] Priya: Yes, I'll send the script and a config that mirrors their rate/sequence distribution.
[05:24] Maya: Also need to check data retention - we don't want logs stored beyond X days for this pilot.
[05:28] Jordan: You can set retention policies in Console for logs; for more strict retention and deletion guarantees Private is the path. We'll include retention options in the security doc.
[05:36] Sam: On support SLAs during pilot - is there any dedicated SE support?
[05:39] Jordan: During the quickstart we provide standard self-serve help and a dedicated SE touch for pilots above a threshold. We'll be your point for getting Priya and the team involved.
[05:48] Liam: Any integration examples for SDK/React/Next?
[05:50] Priya: We have quickstart templates for frontend and backend, a Next.js example that streams tokens to UI, and a server-side batching example.
[05:58] Maya: Great. A couple of micro concerns: tokenization mismatch w/ existing tokenizer tools, and handling of user-supplied safety filters.
[06:06] Priya: We'll provide tokenizer tools and advice; for safety you can apply post-processing hooks or route through a safety filter service; Redwood can integrate with third-party filters.
[06:14] Sam: Sounds good. Let's map concrete next steps.
[06:17] Jordan: Proposed next steps: I send the quickstart guide + credits link, Priya sends benchmark scripts and prompt set, Maya shares a sample dataset and success metrics, then schedule a follow-up in two weeks to review benchmark results.
[06:29] Maya: That works. Also, please include SOC2 report under NDA.
[06:33] Jordan: Will do.
[06:35] Sam: One more question - cost controls for PLG to prevent runaway charges?
[06:39] Jordan: We recommend quotas per team, alerting on spend, and can implement soft caps during the pilot. If you want stricter enforcement, that's part of Dedicated contractual settings.
[06:48] Liam: For the bench we're doing 1000 requests; any rate limit we'll hit on hosted free credits?
[06:52] Priya: Free credits have modest rate limits but sufficient for bench. If you need higher concurrency we'll provision a temporary bump.
[06:58] Maya: Ok sorted.
[07:00] Jordan: I'll recap by email with the links and attachments. Anything else?
[07:04] Sam: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Post-call notes: Natural speech artifacts present (occasional filler, slight speaker misattribution by auto-transcript). Action items and next steps captured above.
